meta.league: Thursday Night Curse Fantasy Football League

2011.title: 2011: The Easel Pad Era
2011.subtitle: Six men, one notepad, and the birth of a curse.
body: 📝 Before the spreadsheets, before the engine, before any of this was taken far too seriously — there was an easel pad. The founding six drafted the inaugural Thursday Night Curse season the old-fashioned way: a marker, a giant paper tablet, and players scrawled out by hand one pick at a time. The drafting was an ordeal, and history records two culprits. Bao 🚬 treated every selection like a hostage negotiation — the man took so long on the clock that the league learned to step outside for a cigarette. Not one. Two. A single Bao pick was reliably a two-smoke affair, and the running joke was born that has never once let him forget it. Then there was Mikey ✍️, less concerned with value than with calligraphy — visibly anxious that his names be written neatly enough for the historical record, hunched over the pad perfecting his penmanship while five grown men heckled him mercilessly.

👑 If there was an early sign of what Hanh would become, it was the High Man of the Week ledger. He hoarded 6 of 17 weekly crowns — a 35% share of the whole season, more than double anyone else — averaging a league-best 114.8 per week against a league average of 108.2, and closing on a ruthless three-week HMOTW run through Weeks 15, 16 and 17 🔥. He was the best week-to-week player in the league. The standings, however, had other ideas right up until the very end.

📈 The standings themselves were a knife fight — just pull up the bump chart above and watch the lines tangle. The early weeks were chaos, with Kito, La and Lonny all trading the top spot. Then Bao, of all people, quietly climbed into first in Week 9 and sat on the throne for four straight weeks. His reign ended the way Bao things tend to: in Week 12 he posted a 90, a 15% drop from his Week 11, and the slow deflation began. Kito pounced, seizing first place and holding it through Weeks 13, 14 and 15 — capped by his 168-point eruption in Week 14, the single highest score of the entire season. He looked, briefly, like a champion.

🗡️ Then came the bump. Hanh had lurked all year, and in Week 16 he vaulted into first by ten points — 1,805 to Kito's 1,794 😬 — a lead he would not surrender. Kito led for three weeks and finished second by 28; he posted the biggest single game of the year and still lost. It was the prologue to a much longer relationship with heartbreak. Behind them, Mikey (1,817) took third on the strength of his impeccably lettered roster, and Bao (1,800) parlayed all that deliberation — and that brief, doomed four-week reign — into a fourth-place finish that was, frankly, more than the smoke breaks deserved.

🎢 And then there is Lonny, whose 2011 is the founding text of a theme this league would return to again and again: HMOTW glory and actual success are not the same race. Lonny caught fire and won three straight weekly titles in Weeks 4, 5 and 6, averaging a scorching 122.0 across that run. The rest of the way? 99.2 🥷. He cooled off by roughly 23 points a week and sank to dead last. Peaking in September and collapsing thereafter is, it turns out, a personality trait, and Lonny established the template before anyone else even knew there was one.

🔮 So the curse was christened: a league where you can hold first place for four weeks and finish fourth, where the best single game of the year belongs to the runner-up, and where the hottest starter finishes last. Hanh got the bragging rights. Everyone else got a story. Fifteen years later, the easel pad is gone, the smoke breaks are a legend, and Mikey's handwriting remains, somewhere, immaculate. Welcome to Thursday Night.

2012.title: 2012: The League Finds Its Legs
2012.subtitle: Expansion, a rookie coronation, and a champion's spectacular face-plant.
body: 🌱 Year two is when the Thursday Night Curse stopped being a six-man lark and became a real league. The roster ballooned to a full ten managers as five newcomers — Damian, Douang, Kevin, Lam and Tony — joined the founders (Lonny, fresh off his last-place 2011, did not return; the template demands sacrifices). The draft, naturally, was still conducted on the sacred easel pad, and naturally Bao 🚬 was still treating the clock as a suggestion. With ten men now waiting on his every pick, his deliberations dragged the whole affair deep into the early morning. The league got its legs in 2012. It also got a permanent sleep deficit.

📊 This is also the year the league grew its brain. 2011 had weekly high scores, but 2012 is when we actually started tracking the High Man of the Week and recording drought streaks — the exact obsession this entire site is now built to memorialize. Fitting that the first season of real tracking produced a worthy inaugural HMOTW king: nobody hoarded weekly crowns like the new guy.

👑 Because the new guy was Damian, and Damian did not come to make friends. In his very first season he won the whole thing — 2,451 points, a league-best 144.2 per week against a 125.7 league average, and a crushing 198-point margin over second place. (For scale: the entire 2011 title was decided by 28 points. Damian won by nearly two hundred.) He seized first place in Week 11 and never surrendered it, and rather than sweat the finish he simply pulled away — his lead swelling to +90 by Week 12 and ballooning to a final +198. He also bullied the new HMOTW ledger for 5.5 weekly crowns, a 32% share of the season. This was not a race. It was a coronation with witnesses.

🤦 And now the part I have to live with. Damian was hesitant to even join this league — and it was me, Hanh, who talked him into it. I personally recruited the man who would walk in off the street and lap the entire field in his rookie year. Worse: remember who won 2011? That would also be me. So the reigning champion spent his title defense escorting his own usurper through the front door — and then put together one of the great collapses in league history, cratering from 1st in 2011 to 9th in 2012 on a sad 1,940 points, below the league average, while the rookie I imported hung banners. Hero to zero in a single calendar year. I would say it never happened again, but hero-to-zero would become one of this league's most reliable traditions. I just had the honor of inventing it.

🎢 Speaking of traditions, 2012 quietly established two more. First, the newcomer-wins-it-all trend — Damian would be the first of several fresh faces to stroll in and steal a title, a recurring indignity the veterans never quite learned to prevent. Second, the Lonny Memorial Last-Place Curse found its next victim in rookie Lam, who finished dead last at 1,898 — and yet, in the season's most on-brand moment, still managed to grab a Week 14 HMOTW crown (153) on his way to the basement. One weekly high, one last-place finish, and then gone: 2012 was Lam's first and only season. He arrived, he peaked for exactly one week, he left. Honestly, a perfect TNCFL career.

🔮 Behind Damian, Douang (2,253) ran second after leading early — he held first as late as Week 10 before Damian's gravity took over — and Mikey (2,198) took third. But make no mistake whose year this was. 2012 gave the league its tenth chair, its drought ledger, and its first cautionary tale about letting talented strangers in the door. Somewhere, Damian is still winning. Somewhere, I am still explaining why I invited him.

2013.title: 2013: The Wheel Turns
2013.subtitle: A champion cast into the pit, a bridesmaid left at the altar, and a man welded to third.
body: ⚖️ If 2012 taught the league that anyone could win, 2013 taught a darker lesson: this league does not love its champions — it devours them. The reigning title holder, Damian, the rookie phenom who had lapped the field by 198 points a year earlier, returned to defend his crown and instead authored one of the most spectacular collapses in TNCFL history. He cratered from 1st (2,451) all the way to DEAD LAST (2,007) — a 444-point freefall — averaging 118.1 per week, a full 22.6 below the league average. From the penthouse to the basement in twelve months. The league offered no sympathy, because the league has no sympathy; humbling last year's king is simply what it does for sport 💀.

🗡️ Into the vacuum stepped Kevin, and his coronation was no cakewalk. He'd finished a forgettable 7th in 2012, and his 2013 title was a grind from the opening whistle — the lead changed hands relentlessly through the first fourteen weeks, with Tony, Hanh, La, Douang and Kevin all taking turns on the throne. Kevin clawed at it the entire way. Then in Week 15 he detonated for 256 — the single highest score of the season — seized first place, and never let go, finishing champion at 2,686 (158.0/wk), 89 clear of second. Up from seventh, through an uphill fight, by way of the biggest game anyone posted all year. Earned, every point.

👰 And in second place, where else, stood Douang. For the second straight year he finished runner-up — 2,597 this time, after 2,253 in 2012 — and for the second straight year he did it while tying for the most HMOTW crowns in the league (5.0, including a three-week tear in Weeks 11–13). More weekly wins than the champion, and still no title. Douang is the eternal bridesmaid of the Thursday Night Curse: always close, always caught, always a step short of the aisle. Forever the prettiest dress in the room and never the one at the altar.

🥉 Which brings us to Mikey, who finished third. As he had in 2012. As he had in 2011. That is three consecutive third-place finishes to open league history — a man so consistent he has essentially turned the bronze medal into assigned seating. Not good enough to win, never bad enough to embarrass himself, Mikey has perfected the art of the podium without the art of the summit. At this point the third-place trophy should just be engraved with his name in advance and his immaculate penmanship used for everyone else's.

📉 As for your humble narrator: Hanh finished 9th (2,276) — my second straight near-basement finish — quietly continuing to pay for the crime of having once been good. Elsewhere, Daniel joined the league as its newest member (a tidy 7th in his debut), filling the chair left by Lam, whose one-and-done 2012 cameo had already passed into legend. The roster held at ten, the scores climbed (a league-average 140.7, up sharply as the managers sharpened), and the wheel kept turning.

🔮 So 2013 set the league's machinery spinning in earnest: a champion devoured, a bridesmaid jilted again, a bronze man bronzed a third time, and a fresh winner pulled up from the middle of the pack. Kevin got the ring — well, the bragging rights; the ring voucher was still two years away — and everyone else got further proof that in this league, the only sure thing is that nothing stays the same except Mikey, who is, was, and evidently always shall be, third.

2014.title: 2014: The Voodoo Doll
2014.subtitle: A hexed champion who couldn't be hexed, a fourth bronze for the ages, and the curse claims another king.
body: 🪆 Every league needs an origin myth, and 2014's was forged out of pure desperation. Early on, La — watching yet another fast start from the front of the pack — floated the idea of a voodoo doll: a little effigy of the league leader to be poked, jabbed and cursed into a slump. It was a joke. Mostly. And it had exactly one target all season long, because one man grabbed the lead and simply would not give it back. The league poked. The league prayed. The league jabbed that doll into splinters. It did absolutely nothing.

👑 That man was Randy, and — say it with me now — he won it all in his very first season. The second rookie in three years to walk in off the street and seize the title, Randy made it look insulting: 2,761 points, a league-best 162.4 per week (the field averaged 137.1), and a 208-point demolition of second place. He took over first in Week 4 and never surrendered it — 14 straight weeks on the throne — piling up a league-high 4.5 HMOTW crowns including a 216-point haymaker in Week 8. Every voodoo pin La pushed in only seemed to make him stronger. (We didn't know it yet, but we were jabbing at the man who would become the biggest money-earner in league history. The doll never stood a chance. More on Randy's reign of terror in the seasons to come.)

🔪 The cruelest irony? The doll's only victim was its own creator. La finished second (2,553) — close enough to taste it, cursed enough to never reach it. A man invents a hex for the league leader and the only fortune he alters is his own, into runner-up. Somewhere in that is a lesson about karma. Mostly it's just funny.

🥉 And now we must speak, with appropriate reverence, of Mikey. For in 2014 he finished third. Again. Those keeping score at home: that is third, third, third, AND third — FOUR consecutive bronze finishes to open league history, a feat of such relentless, machine-tooled mediocrity that it transcends failure and becomes legend. Mikey does not chase trophies; he reports to the third-place step like it's a shift he clocks into. Four years running he has found the podium and, with the precision of a man who knows his place, planted himself firmly on its lowest rung. They say you can't script consistency. Mikey is a four-act play with the same ending. The bronze is no longer an award — it's his property.

💀 Meanwhile, the throne kept eating its occupants. Kevin, the reigning 2013 champion, defended his title by collapsing to 9th (2,000), below the league average — the third straight year a defending champ was dragged from the penthouse to the cellar (Hanh in '12, Damian in '13, now Kevin). By now it is not a fluke; it is the central law of the Thursday Night Curse. Win the title and the league marks you. The crown is not a reward here — it's a target painted on your back, and every season the curse collects its tribute from the man foolish enough to have been best. Damian, for his part, clawed off the canvas from dead-last to a respectable 5th; small mercies.

🚬 Two more notes for the ledger. Douang, the two-time bridesmaid, finally missed the wedding entirely, sliding from back-to-back runner-up to a distant 6th — even heartbreak, it seems, expires. And we bid a temporary farewell to Bao, the patron saint of the two-smoke draft pick, absent this season after closing out 2013 as his last. He'll be back for one more cursed cameo down the road, but that's a drought story for another year. As for your narrator, Hanh climbed to 7th — my best finish since the founding title, which tells you everything about how the mighty had fallen. Progress is progress. The voodoo doll, mercifully, was never pointed at me. There was no need.

2015.title: 2015: The Bronze Medalist Ascends
2015.subtitle: A founder finally breaks through, a record drought rains out, and the league sets a new floor for misery.
body: 👑 For four long years the Thursday Night Curse belonged to the newcomers — Damian, Kevin, Randy strolling in off the street and walking out with crowns while the founders watched from the cheap seats. In 2015, the old guard finally bit back, and it came from the unlikeliest place imaginable: the bronze step. Mikey — owner of an absurd FOUR straight third-place finishes to open league history, a man who reported to the podium's lowest rung like a shift he clocked into — abandoned his reserved spot and climbed all the way to the top, winning his first championship at 2,580 points. He didn't back into it, either: Mikey posted a league-best 151.8 points per week against a 140.3 average, the most complete season of his career. The man who couldn't escape third place suddenly couldn't be caught.

🗡️ It was, however, a knife fight to the wire. Mikey actually grabbed first as early as Week 4, then watched it slip through a long, nervous midsection where he sat stubbornly in third for six straight weeks. The dam broke in Week 13: he reclaimed the lead and refused to surrender it, fending off a furious Tony, who finished second by a mere 43 points (2,537). It was Tony's best finish in league history by a country mile, fueled by a league-leading 4 weekly High Man crowns — a genuine breakout that announced him as a real contender. Behind them, Daniel claimed third (2,487), a quiet career year of his own. And then came the headline nobody saw coming: Kito, of all people, finished fourth.

🌧️ Yes — THAT Kito. The patron saint of the A-KITO-cama Desert, the man who had gone a league-record 45 weeks without a single weekly win, finally got his rain. He won three HMOTWs in 2015, broke the drought that had defined three full seasons of his life, and parlayed the resurrection into a 4th-place finish and his first paycheck in years (+$94). The rain dance, it turns out, works — you just have to keep stomping for the better part of a decade with the entire league laughing at you. Somewhere, a fantasy god finally blinked, sighed, and turned on the sprinklers.

💀 If Kito found mercy, the league extracted its toll elsewhere, and it extracted it with interest. La — the 2014 runner-up, a man who'd been a whisker from a title the year before — fell straight off a cliff, finishing dead last (2,061) and posting, in Week 10, a 58: the lowest single-week score in league history, a record for misery that still stands today, unthreatened. He took the season's worst financial beating at -$444. From the silver podium to the all-time floor in twelve months; the Curse, as ever, keeps a level ledger and a very long memory.

💸 And the throne kept biting the hand that fed it. Randy, the reigning 2014 rookie champion, defended his title by sinking to 9th (2,165) — the fourth straight year a defending champ was dragged from the penthouse to the cellar (Hanh in '12, Damian in '13, Kevin in '14, now Randy). By now it is not a fluke or a coincidence; it is the central, load-bearing law of the Thursday Night Curse. Win the title and the league marks you. The crown is not a reward here — it is a target painted on your back, collected on without fail the following autumn. Mikey, you have been warned: enjoy the view, because next year the doll comes for you.

🔮 So 2015 will be remembered as the year the founders remembered how to win, the year the longest drought in league history finally broke, and the year a man scored 58 points and lived to tell the tale. Mikey got his ring after four years of bridesmaid bronze. Kito got his rain after three years in the sand. La got the record nobody wants and a -$444 invoice to go with it. And the Curse, fed and satisfied, dusted off its hands and went looking for next year's king.

2016.title: 2016: The Lazarus Season
2016.subtitle: A former champion claws back from the grave, the closest podium in league history, and the curse keeps its perfect record.
body: 👑 In 2012, Damian walked in as a rookie and won the whole thing by nearly 200 points. In 2013, the Curse collected its tribute and dropped him to dead last. Two quiet seasons in the wilderness followed — 5th, then 7th — and the league quietly wrote him off as a one-hit wonder, a kid who'd gotten lucky once. Then came 2016, and the greatest resurrection in Thursday Night history. After a sluggish start that had him sitting 8th and 9th through the opening fortnight, Damian found another gear, surged into first in Week 9, and never surrendered the lead again — reclaiming the crown at 2,624 points on a thunderous 154.4 average against a 139.9 league mark. From champion to basement to champion again. Lazarus had nothing on him.

💣 The engine of the comeback was a brutal midseason one-two punch: 205 in Week 9, 200 in Week 10 — and the timing was perfect, because 2016 was the year the league introduced the Double High Man of the Week. Crack 200 points in a week and you don't just win the weekly pot, you win it doubled — a rule the managers funded by bumping their weekly premiums from $10 to $20. Damian didn't just inaugurate the era; he ran it, posting the first two DHMOTWs in league history on back-to-back weeks at the exact moment he seized the throne. He paired the fireworks with a league-best 5.5 weekly crowns and, by the time the dust settled, a colossal +$1,297 — one of the fattest single-season hauls the league had ever paid out, a fitting bounty for a man returning from the dead.

🏎️ But oh, the chase behind him. 2016 produced the tightest podium in league history: Damian 2,624, Kevin 2,555, Randy 2,544 — Kevin edging Randy for second by a cruel, rounding-error 11 points. Both played championship-caliber football all year long; both watched a resurrected man hoist the trophy. Kevin's +$657 and Randy's sneak into the money at third (+$118) were lovely consolation prizes for a two-man race decided by less than a single good drive — eleven points they will both replay in their heads for years.

💀 And the throne, as ever, devoured its last occupant. Mikey — who had finally broken through for his maiden title in 2015 after four years of bronze — defended it by tumbling all the way to 7th, the fifth consecutive year a reigning champion collapsed the season after winning (Hanh, Damian, Kevin, Randy, now Mikey). The pattern is no longer remarkable; it is load-bearing, structural, a law as dependable as gravity. The crown remains the single most dangerous thing a man can win in this league — a one-year lease on glory with a guaranteed eviction notice stapled to it.

🌵 Spare a thought, too, for Kito. One year removed from finally breaking his record 45-week drought and climbing to a respectable 4th, he came crashing right back to dead last (2,117), swallowing the season's worst loss at -$450. The rain came in 2015; in 2016 the desert reclaimed its favorite son and bolted the door behind him. And quietly, in the background, Tony — the breakout runner-up of 2015 — went 23 weeks without a weekly win and inherited the drought crown, proof that in this league a great year is often just the elaborate setup for the punchline. The cellar and the desert are always hiring, and the pay is terrible.

🔮 2016, then: the year the dead came back to rule, the year second place was decided by a rounding error, and the year the defending-champion curse went a perfect five-for-five. Damian got his redemption and the fattest check in the house. Kevin and Randy got heartbreak by eleven points and a long offseason to stew on it. Mikey got the doll. And the Thursday Night Curse, undefeated as always and bored of being doubted, simply kept score.

2017.title: 2017: The Narrator's Revenge
2017.subtitle: The founding champion ends a six-year exile, the curse finally blinks, and your humble storyteller gets the last laugh.
body: 👑 Allow me a rare moment of immodesty. For six years I have narrated this league's carnage from the cheap seats, chronicling other men's titles while my own founding crown gathered dust and my finishes read like a countdown to irrelevance: 9th, 9th, 7th, 8th, 8th. The 2011 champion had become the league's resident historian, a man who wrote beautifully about winning and did precious little of it. But here is the one stat I'll defend to the grave: I don't always make the podium — but when I do, it's all the way to the top. Two podium finishes in seven years, and both of them first place. No silver, no bronze, no consolation — just titles. And in 2017 I made the climb again, winning the whole thing at 2,491 points for my second championship, six full years after the first.

🔥 It was no fluke, either. I led the league with 5 weekly High Man crowns and posted a 146.5 average against a 134.7 league mark — the best season I'd put together since the founding year. The path wasn't a straight line: I grabbed first early in Weeks 3 and 4, lost it through a choppy midsection, and seized it back for good in Week 16, holding on through the finish. After half a decade of writing other men's glory, I finally had a story of my own to tell.

🗡️ And what a finish it was — the second photo-finish podium in as many years. Hanh 2,491, Damian 2,437, Mikey 2,434: I held off the field by 54, while behind me Damian edged Mikey for second by an excruciating 3 points. Mikey, the 2015 champion, once again found himself a hair short of the silver — some men collect bronze, and some collect near-misses, and Mikey has somehow made a career of both. Either way the man cannot catch a break in a tiebreaker; he has now finished within a single possession of a better placement more times than anyone cares to count.

🔗 The bigger news may have been what DIDN'T happen. For five straight years, the reigning champion had collapsed the season after winning — an iron law of the Curse, paid out every autumn without exception (Hanh '12, Damian '13, Kevin '14, Randy '15, Mikey '16). In 2017, Damian broke it: the defending 2016 champ followed his title with a second-place finish, the first time in league history a titleholder backed up his crown with another podium. After half a decade of devouring its kings, the Curse finally blinked. Whether that's genuine mercy or merely the Curse changing its diet remains very much to be seen.

🏜️ Down at the other end, the misery found new tenants. Kevin cratered to dead last (2,072), bookending his year with a 65 in Week 9 and a 68 in the opener, and absorbing a -$402 beating. And the drought crown passed to an unlikely heir: Randy, the 2014 rookie champion, closed the year on a 26-week HMOTW drought — the longest active streak in the league. The kid who once arrived like a monsoon now rules a desert. The Curse, it seems, keeps its receipts on everyone.

💵 2017 also debuted a brand-new way to lose money: the Winner-Take-All side bet. The rules are gloriously simple — any manager who wants in throws an extra $100 into a pot, and whoever among them racks up the most total points by season's end takes the entire thing. Seven brave souls anted up, building a $700 pool — and wouldn't you know it, the same man having his career-best season scooped it. Yours truly won the inaugural WTA, turning my title run into a side-pot sweep and folding a tidy $700 into the season's haul. When it rains, friends, it pours — and in 2017, for once, it rained on me.

🔮 So 2017 will go in the books as the year the historian became the headline. After six years in the wilderness, the founding champion came home — five weekly crowns, a second title, and the first ring of his career. (When I won in 2011 the league hadn't yet ponied up for ring vouchers; that didn't start until 2015, so the founding crown came with bragging rights and bare knuckles. This time I finally got the hardware.) The fat +$1,827 payday — WTA pot included — didn't hurt either, and it silenced the doubters — most of them, admittedly, also me. The defending-champ curse cracked, Mikey lost another tiebreaker, and Randy inherited the sand. As for your narrator: I came, I saw, I finally shut up and won. We now return you to your regularly scheduled humility.

2018.title: 2018: From the Sand to the Summit
2018.subtitle: The reigning drought king reinvents himself as champion, the points pour down in a record flood, and one man stays bone dry through all of it.
body: 👑 A year ago, Randy was the punchline — the 2014 rookie champion reduced to ruling the Sa-RANDY Desert on a 26-week High Man drought, the driest man in the league. What a difference twelve months makes. In 2018 Randy didn't just escape the sand; he conquered the whole map, storming to his second championship at 2,793 points on a colossal 164.3-point average against a 146.5 league mark. He grabbed the lead for good in Week 10 and never flinched. From driest man alive to undisputed champion in a single calendar — the most complete reinvention the league had seen since Damian rose from the dead.

📈 And what a year to do it in. 2018 was the highest-scoring season in league history, a relentless points flood that turned the new Double High Man rule into a fireworks show. Six separate weeks saw a winner crack 200 and bank a doubled pot: Mikey opened with 206 in Week 1, Randy answered with 205 in Week 2, Damian went off twice (209 and 202), Kevin posted 207, and Kito dropped the single biggest game of the year — a 210 in Week 7. Three years earlier the DHMOTW had debuted with a grand total of two such weeks; in 2018 the league tripled it. The arms race had arrived.

🥈 Spare, once again, a thought for Mikey. He posted a monster season of his own — 2,747 points, tied for the league lead with five weekly crowns — and still came up 46 points short, finishing second. It is becoming the defining trait of his career: brilliant, relentless, and forever a step behind at the line. The 2015 champion has now turned the runner-up and bronze slots into a personal timeshare, collecting near-misses the way other men collect rings. Some players chase the trophy; Mikey seems cosmically doomed to finish within arm's reach of it and grab nothing but air.

🏜️ But while one desert king escaped, another simply refused to leave. Tony — who first took up residence in the So-TONY-ran Desert back in 2016 — turned his long-term lease into permanent ownership, closing 2018 on a punishing 30-week drought and finishing dead last. The cruelty was almost artful: in the single highest-scoring season the league had ever played, with 200-point weeks raining down on everyone in sight, Tony went the entire year without a weekly crown. A man standing in a monsoon, holding an empty bucket, watching the whole league get soaked while he stayed bone dry.

💀 The rest of the bottom was its own quiet carnage. Defending 2017 champion Hanh did exactly what defending champions do around here — slid to 8th, the curse reasserting itself one year after Damian briefly cracked it. And the money ran red below the podium: Tony's -$592 and Hanh's -$580 were the season's deepest wounds, the price of a year spent watching everyone else hang touchdowns. The points were everywhere in 2018; they just weren't evenly distributed.

🔮 So 2018 stands as the league's loudest, highest-scoring season yet — the year the drought king became the champion, the year the Double High Man rule turned into a weekly fireworks display, and the year one stubborn man stayed dry through the wettest season on record. Randy got his redemption and a fat +$1,668 to frame it. Mikey got another silver to add to the collection. Tony got the sand, again. And the Curse, watching the points pile up to record heights, simply smiled and kept its books.

2019.title: 2019: The Long Way Home
2019.subtitle: The man with one weekly crown all year wins the whole thing, a founder returns to bury a record drought, and the league's most dominant manager somehow ends up with everything but the ring.
body: 👑 Some debts take eight years to collect. Back in the founding season of 2011, Kito led down the stretch, posted the biggest game of the year, then watched Hanh vault past him in Week 16 to steal the inaugural crown by 28. So savor the symmetry of 2019: Kito won the whole thing at 2,648 points (a league-best 155.8 average vs. 145.0) — and he did it by overtaking the leader in Week 16, the same week he'd once been overtaken. Here's the kicker: Kito won exactly one High Man crown all season, his lone eruption a 205 in Week 15. He spent the entire year parked in second or third, never the weekly headline, just relentlessly there. The man who used to score the most and win the least flipped the curse inside out — fewest crowns, the only title that counts.

🏁 And oh, the man he overtook. Randy, the defending champion, didn't lead 2019 so much as own it. He won five of the first seven weeks — a three-peat in Weeks 1–3, then Weeks 5 and 7 — including a 216-point double-double in Week 5, the season's biggest game. He held first place for fifteen unbroken weeks, averaging a frankly unfair 168.78 through Week 9 before cooling to 134.88 the rest of the way. And those fifteen weeks were only the back half of something bigger: Randy had also closed out his 2018 title defense on top, so his reign at first actually stretched 23 straight weeks — from 2018 Week 10 all the way through 2019 Week 15 — the longest unbroken run at the top in league history, and the only one ever to span two seasons. Then Kito caught him in Week 16 and shut the door, and Randy — the most dominant manager in the league, in a league he led for fifteen weeks — finished second by 50. As the blog of the day put it: to beat Randy, his whole team had to die. It nearly didn't happen at all.

💸 Here is where 2019 turns gloriously cruel. By every weekly measure Randy WAS the best player in the field — most crowns, biggest game, fifteen weeks in first — and the Curse paid him in everything except the trophy. Seven men anted up $100 apiece for the Winner-Take-All pot, $700 to the highest total scorer among them, and Randy swept it clean. The arithmetic stings: his +$1,427.90 haul — second-place money plus the side pot — dwarfed champion Kito's +$885.20. The man who lost the title walked out the single richest manager in the league. Don't cry for him, Argentina.

🌦️ The desert, meanwhile, gave up two of its oldest prisoners. Bao — the two-smoke-pick founder of the easel-pad era, back after a five-year absence (last seen in 2013) — walked into the league and in Week 4 promptly ended the longest drought in league history: 96 weeks. The all-time record, buried by the very man who set it, in his fourth game back. Five weeks later Tony escaped too, his 193 in Week 9 snapping a 38-week drought — 758 calendar days, by the blog's reverent count. Two deserts closed in a single season. The sand never empties for long, but for a few weeks in 2019 it actually rained on the right people.

🆕 No one rode the season's whiplash like the rookies and comeback kids. Ted debuted with the full bipolar range of this league: the season's lowest game, a 75 in Week 4, then a Week 6 crown, then a 200-point DHMOTW in Week 8, climbing to 2nd by Week 12 on a blistering 160.88 average. Cruelest of all, he sat inside the money circle most of the year and got bumped out at the final gun — Damian's Week 17 High Man (his second, after Week 14) leapfrogged into 4th and kicked the rookie out of the cash. And La, the comeback kid, sat between 8th and 10th from Week 5 through Week 15, dead in the water — then two monster weeks, a 206 in Week 16 among them, catapulted the La Ness Monster to third, edging Damian for the final podium by a heart-stopping 9 points (2,493 to 2,484).

🔮 So 2019 goes in the books as the year the league's most decorated loser finally won. Kito came the long way home — one crown, eight years, a lifetime of near-misses — and took his first title with a Week 16 ambush that rhymed perfectly with the one that broke his heart in 2011. Randy got fifteen weeks in first, five early crowns, the biggest game, the WTA pot, and the largest payday in the league — everything except the ring. Bao and Tony got their rain at last. And down at the bottom, a familiar drumbeat: Kevin closed the year bone dry on a 21-week High Man drought, the league's new driest man on severe drought watch, with the freshly-rained-on Bao kicking up dust right behind him. The desert never closes; it just changes the name on the lease.

2020.title: 2020: Wire to Wire in a Burning Year
2020.subtitle: In the season nobody was sure would happen, the narrator leads from the first whistle to the last, a rookie comes within two points of the silver, and the record book gets rewritten in a pandemic.
body: 👑 Permit your historian one more immodest entry. The running joke has always been that I don't always make the podium — but when I do, it's all the way to the top. Through 2019 that was two-for-two: 2011 and 2017, both firsts, no silver, no bronze. In 2020 I made it three-for-three. I won at 2,710 points, and did it the hard way and the easy way at once: I grabbed first in Week 1 and never let go, leading wire to wire, all 17 weeks — the first gate-to-tape title the league had ever seen, and the longest single-season reign at first the league has ever produced. I'll grant Randy his due, though: his 23-week run atop the standings (2018 Week 10 through 2019 Week 15) remains the longest consecutive reign in league history — the only one ever to bridge two seasons. He held first longer; I held it an entire season without interruption. We can each keep our record. There's a milestone in it beyond the gloat, too: since the league started handing out ring vouchers in 2015, every champion had been a different man — Mikey, Damian, me, Randy, Kito, one apiece. My 2020 title (on top of 2017) makes me the first manager to earn TWO rings in the voucher era. After a decade of narrating other men's glory between my own droughts, I led every single week of a championship and stacked a second ring. Allow me this one. I've earned the gloat.

🦠 And what a year to do it in. 2020 was the season nobody was sure would even happen — a pandemic-shadowed schedule with contingency math drawn up in case COVID truncated the year, ESPN roster rules bent on the fly, and a GroupMe that ran hotter than the games. We played all seventeen weeks anyway, and it became one of the best on record. The points poured: the league averaged 146.8 a week, and the Double High Man rule went off seven times — a new record, one past 2018's flood — with 200-plus weeks from Hanh (twice), Mikey (twice), Kito (twice), and La. A burning year outside; a fireworks show inside.

🔥 The points poured all over the field, and nobody poured harder than Kito. The reigning champion spent 2020 on a one-man assault: a 215 in Week 14, then a Week 16 222-point eruption — at the time the second-highest single week the league had ever seen, trailing only Kevin's all-time-record 256 from 2013. The two biggest games of the 2020 season were both his, and he tied for the league lead with five weekly crowns. And — most Kito of all — he still didn't win. He fell as far as 9th in Week 6 before clawing back, and took second by a 28-point margin behind me. The man drops the year's two biggest games and pockets the silver. Some things never change.

🆕 The story of the year, though, was the fresh meat. D'lyn — "Dilly Dilly," the rookie — walked into the most competitive league in the state and nearly stole the whole thing in his first season. He surged from 6th into the money by Week 6, claimed 2nd place by Week 12, and held it for five straight weeks with the title in his sights, trading High Man near-misses with me down the stretch. Then a couple of cruel coaching decisions in the final game — a benched quarterback at exactly the wrong moment — cost him both placements: he finished third, just 2 points behind Kito for silver and 30 behind me for the ring. Rookies winning is practically a league tradition — Damian did it in 2012, Randy in 2014 — but a fresh face going stride-for-stride for the crown into the final hour, and missing the silver by a field goal, is its own kind of arrival. Welcome to the league, kid. It will break your heart and you'll keep coming back.

🏈 2020 also gave the league its first-ever playoff — a bracket bolted onto the back of the season. Mikey rode a hot Mahomes-and-Hill tandem through the field and edged Kevin in the inaugural Superbowl on a Fournette flex-score tiebreaker, pocketing $350 to Kevin's $100 — the kind of new wrinkle 2020 specialized in. And the transaction pot, swollen by a captive pandemic audience refreshing the waiver wire, ballooned to a record $2,913 — which, with the $1,000 side pot I also swept, made the fattest single-season payday in league history: +$2,098.20.

🌦️ And the desert, as ever, kept its books on the fallen. The cruelest reversal belonged to Randy: a year removed from leading 2019 for fifteen weeks, he cratered to dead-last earnings (-$667) and inherited the longest active drought in the league — 27 weeks dry, the Sa-RANDY Desert reopened for business, with Ted (26 weeks) baking right beside him. Damian took the hardest competitive fall, collapsing to last place (2,011) and posting the season's lowest game, a 72 in Week 10. So 2020 closes as the year the narrator finally led one start to finish, a rookie nearly toppled a decade of veterans, Kito posted the year's two biggest games and still lost, and the league threw a playoff party in the middle of a pandemic. We needed the distraction. It delivered.

2021.title: 2021: The Rookie Wrecking Ball
2021.subtitle: The veterans should have learned by now. A first-year manager strolls in, leads sixteen straight weeks, and laps the field — while last year's record-setter falls all the way to the cellar.
body: 👑 The league has a recurring nightmare, and its name keeps changing. Damian lived it in 2012, Randy in 2014, and in 2021 a new face wrote the latest chapter: Titi, a rookie, who didn't just win the league in his first season — he obliterated it. He grabbed first place in Week 3 and never let go, leading the standings for sixteen straight weeks to a 2,978.7-point title, the highest-scoring championship the league had ever produced. His winning margin was a staggering 158.6 points — the most lopsided title since Damian's own rookie blowout in 2012. He led the league with 6 High Man crowns, including back-to-back DHMOTW explosions in Weeks 3 and 5. The veterans circled the new kid all year and never laid a glove on him. Welcome to the league, Titi. You've already ruined everyone's plans.

🆕 2021 was a season of arrivals and departures both. The league finally expanded to an 18-week regular season, and two fresh faces took the chairs left empty by La and Mikey, who stepped away after a decade. One newcomer, Titi, walked straight to the throne. The other, Tim, walked straight into the desert — more on his parched rookie year shortly. It was the biggest single-season roster turnover since the 2012 expansion, and it reshaped the league's competitive order overnight: of the ten men who finished, the two at the very top of the standings were a rookie and a near-rookie story, and the bottom was littered with men who used to own the place.

🔥 Nobody fell harder than Kito. Twelve months after a year for the ages — the 2019 championship, the 2020 silver, the 222-point eruption — the reigning runner-up came back in 2021 and finished dead last (2,507.8). He even opened the season with the year's single biggest game, a 235.5 in Week 1 (second only, in league history, to Kevin's all-time 256 from 2013), and somehow turned that fast start into a face-plant, going winless from Week 2 onward and sliding to the cellar. The defending-champion curse has many victims, but rarely has it dropped a man so far so fast: from the silver podium and a scoring record to the basement in a single calendar.

💪 The rebound of the year belonged to Randy, who arrived at 2021 as the reigning punchline — the man who'd led 2019 for fifteen weeks, then cratered to a 27-week drought and last-place earnings in 2020. He answered with a vengeance: a strong second-place finish (2,820.1), three weekly crowns, and a return to the money that pushed him to +$1,162.30 on the year. He broke his own drought and ended the season bone-dry to nobody — zero weeks since his last crown. From driest man in the league to runner-up in twelve months. In a league this cruel, redemption is just the setup for the next fall, but Randy earned this one.

🏜️ And the bottom of the rain chart told its own grim story. Tim, the OTHER rookie, endured the polar opposite of Titi's coronation: he went his entire 18-week debut season without a single High Man crown, finishing 9th and inheriting the league's longest active drought at 18 weeks. Right behind him sat the fallen champion Kito (17 weeks dry), giving the desert an odd couple for the ages — the winless newcomer and the deposed king, baking side by side. Up the standings, the middle was a knife fight: Tony (3rd), Kevin (4th), and Ted (5th) finished within 45 points of one another, with Tony edging into the money by a comfortable margin and Ted missing the cash by a single good quarter.

🔮 So 2021 goes in the books as the year the rookie wrecking ball came through. Titi led sixteen weeks, won by 159, and walked off with a record-scoring title and a +$1,590.40 payday in his very first season — proof, yet again, that in this league experience is no defense against a hungry newcomer. Randy got his redemption and the silver; Tony snuck onto the podium; and Kito, the man who had everything in 2019 and 2020, got the cellar and a spot in the desert next to a rookie who never won a thing. The 18-week era opened exactly the way the league always does: with the veterans humbled and a fresh face holding the ring. Some lessons, apparently, never take.

2022.title: 2022: The Long Way to the Top
2022.subtitle: The man the league spent years roasting for his droughts finally answered back — Tony seized the lead in Week 1 and, but for two stray Thursdays, never let it go, turning an eleven-year wait into a front-running coronation.
body: 👑 Every league has a manager it loves to tease, and for the better part of a decade that man was Tony. He debuted in 2012 and spent his prime collecting cellar finishes — 8th, 9th, 10th, 9th — and getting his own desert named after him not once but twice (the So-TONY-ran, 2016 and 2018). His only flirtations with glory were a 2015 runner-up and a 2021 bronze. Then 2022 happened. Tony grabbed first place in Week 1 and held the top of the standings for 16 of 18 weeks, finishing at 2,972.24 points — the league's best — for his first championship in eleven seasons and his first-ever ring.

🏁 He made it look easy, but it wasn't airtight. Tony slipped to 2nd in Week 2 as Titi briefly grabbed the top spot, and again to 2nd in Week 13 when Kito nosed in front for a single Thursday. Both times Tony answered immediately, reclaiming the lead the very next week and never trailing otherwise. Kito chased him to the wire, settling for 2nd at 2,919.30 — a final margin of just 52.94 points across eighteen weeks. Ted banked the steadiest year of his career for 3rd (2,814.02), and 2021's wrecking-ball rookie Titi rounded out the money in 4th (2,765.20).

💥 If the standings belonged to Tony, the weekly fireworks belonged to two other men. Kito and Titi tied for the season HMOTW lead with 7.0 tallies apiece, trading High Man crowns from the opening whistle. Titi struck first with a doubled pot in Week 2 (203.08) and posted the season's biggest game — 219.44 in Week 8 — while Kito answered with doublers in Weeks 5 (217.22) and 7 (208.86). Tony, fittingly for a champion who won on grind rather than ceiling, managed only 5.0 tallies of his own and cracked the weekly top three just nine times — he simply never had a bad enough week to lose the lead.

🎰 The 200-point club met often: six weeks cleared the doubled-pot threshold, two of them with multiple managers over 200, and both times the rule paid only the high man. In Week 5, Kito's 217.22 edged Tony's 204.28; in Week 8, Titi's 219.44 beat Ted's 208.40. For all the explosions, none threatened the record books — Titi's 219.44 ranks just 6th all-time through 2022, with Kevin's 256 (2013) still standing untouched.

💵 The money was a story all its own. Tony didn't merely win the season — he ran the table. He took the $1,162.80 champion's purse (prize plus the $250 ring voucher), swept the $1,000 sidebet pool as the highest cumulative scorer of all ten entrants, and added $100 as playoff runner-up, for a staggering net of +$2,114.80. But the one ring he couldn't get was the playoff crown: for the second straight year Tony reached the playoff Superbowl and lost it — beaten by Titi in 2021, and this time by Randy, a 5th-place regular season who ran the manual bracket for the $400 champion's share. Also new in 2022: the player-received fee quietly dropped from $5 to $2.

🏜️ And then there was the rain dance. While Tony danced on the podium, Tim was still out in the desert. A year after going winless through his entire 18-week rookie season, Tim stayed bone-dry all of 2022, stretching his active drought to 36 weeks — the longest earned-while-active streak in the whole league at season's end. He wasn't alone in the sand: Ted carried 26 dry weeks despite his bronze finish, and D'lyn 22. But Tim owned the wasteland, and the ledger agreed — his -$636 was second only to D'lyn's -$664 at the bottom of the table. The veterans had a new champion to chase, and the rookies had a desert to escape.

2023.title: 2023: The Tim Takeover
2023.subtitle: After going winless for two full seasons, Tim didn’t just break his drought — he broke everything in sight, winning the standings, the weekly crown, the sidebet, and the ring in one of the most complete seasons any manager has ever put together.
body: 🏜️ Coming into 2023, Tim owned one distinction nobody wanted: the longest drought to start his fantasy career in the league at 36 weeks across two entire winless seasons. He had never won a single HMOTW crown since his debut in 2021-W01. The league had a name for his desert. His rain-dance card had run two consecutive years. The question for 2023 wasn’t whether Tim could win — it was whether he could survive another year of being the punchline.

💧 Week 4 answered that. Amid a chaotic opening stretch where Hanh led Week 1, Kevin led Week 2, and Kito fired off the season’s first doubled pot in Week 3 with a 206.70, Tim stepped through the noise and won his first-ever HMOTW crown in Week 4 with 182.26 — ending a 39-week drought dating back to his very first career week. He didn’t stop. He won again in Week 6, reached the top of the standings for the first time in Week 8, and from Week 10 onward never left first place — leading the final 9 straight weeks to close out the season.

🏁 Kevin made it interesting early, holding first from Weeks 4 through 7 and returning briefly in Week 9 before Tim locked the door. Kevin’s back half faded badly and he settled for 4th at 2,716.92. The final podium ended up absurdly tight: Ted finished 2nd at 2,742.90 and Damian took 3rd at 2,741.08 — just 1.82 points separating them after 18 weeks. Behind them Kevin sat only 25.16 points further back. The bottom three spots of the money were decided by a margin narrower than a single good quarter.

💥 Tim’s dominance wasn’t just a standings story. He led the league in HMOTW tally at 7.0, including back-to-back doubled pots in Weeks 12 (209.64) and 15 (203.70). Damian was the second crown-chaser at 5.0, winning four times including a 202.90 in Week 8. The season delivered six DHMOTW weeks, with Randy landing the season’s biggest game — 225.64 in Week 16. Tony, the defending champion, tallied exactly zero HMOTW crowns all season. Not one.

💵 The financial sweep was total. Tim won the $944 season prize, pocketed the $250 ring voucher, collected $700 in HMOTW earnings, and swept the $1,000 sidebet pool as the highest cumulative scorer — a net of +$2,232, the second-largest single-season haul in league history. In the playoff bracket, all ten managers paid in for a $500 pool. The bracket produced the season’s best punchline: D’lyn, who finished 5th in the standings and spent most of the year as the league’s longest active drought holder, walked away as playoff champion and pocketed $400 — his best financial year to date.

🏆 The drought ironies closed the book on 2023. Tim ended a 39-week desert and immediately became the league’s best player. D’lyn snapped his own 39-week drought on the very last game of the regular season — Week 18, 189.92 — tying Tim and the long-departed Douang for the 4th-longest streak in league history. And Tony, who spent eleven years chasing his first ring and finally got it in 2022, closed 2023 as the thirstiest man standing at 21 straight dry weeks. The defending-champ curse had claimed another. Somewhere in the inactive wilderness, Mikey’s streak ticked past 59 weeks without a soul noticing.

2024.title: 2024: The Randy Rampage
2024.subtitle: Randy didn’t just win 2024 — he rewrote the record books, setting the all-time marks for single-season HMOTW tally, total net earnings, and DHMOTW weeks in a performance that left the rest of the league watching from a distance.
body: 🏜️ The 2024 season had one story and one storyteller. Randy grabbed first place in Week 4 and essentially never let go, leading the cumulative standings for 12 of 18 weeks and finishing at 3,104.20 points — the highest season total in league history. His nearest rival was Hanh, who led briefly in Weeks 3, 9, 10, and 14 before Randy reasserted each time. After Week 11 the race was over in everything but name.

🔥 The headline number was Randy’s 10.0 HMOTW tally — an all-time league record by a margin of three full crowns over the previous best of 7.0. Randy won in Weeks 4, 5, 7, 15, 16, and 17, with four of those being doubled pots. His closing run of three straight DHMOTWs — 215.58 (Wk 15), 203.44 (Wk 16), and 221.54 (Wk 17) — put an exclamation point on a season that was already decided. In Week 5 he had company over 200: Tim posted 202.52 the same week, but the rule pays only the high man and Randy’s 204.36 took it.

💥 The season was the most explosive in league history by raw volume: nine DHMOTW weeks, shattering the prior record of seven set in 2020. Three of those weeks featured multiple managers over 200 — Wk 5 (Randy and Tim), Wk 11 (Damian and D’lyn), and Wk 15 (Randy and Tony) — with the rule each time awarding the doubled pot to the single weekly high. The biggest single game of the year was Damian’s 233.60 in Week 11 — the 3rd-highest single-week score in league history, behind only Kevin’s 256 (2013) and Kito’s 235 (2021).

👑 The money was unprecedented. Randy took the $908 season prize, the $250 ring voucher, $1,000 in HMOTW earnings, swept the $1,000 sidebet pool as the highest cumulative scorer, and won the playoff bracket for $400 — a net of +$2,902, the largest single-season take in the fourteen-year history of this league. Hanh was the only other manager in the black at +$519, collecting the runner-up prize and 5.0 HMOTW tally. The defending champion Tim finished a respectable 3rd (2,827.96) — a sharp contrast to the four previous title-holders who each finished 6th or worse the year after their crown.

🆕 The season also introduced a new face. Aidan made his league debut in 2024, won his first HMOTW crown in Week 6 (180.66), and finished 9th (2,512.60). Meanwhile at the bottom of the table, Kito had one of the worst statistical seasons in league history: 0 HMOTW tally, 10th place (2,394.50), and 11 weeks spent in last place in the cumulative standings. His drought stretched to 33 weeks by season’s end.

🌊 The wider league picture was one of compression at the top and collapse at the bottom. Tony (4th, 2,749.44), D’lyn (5th, 2,732.48), and Ted (6th, 2,726.08) finished within 23 points of each other in spots 4 through 6. Randy’s dominance meant five managers finished in the red by more than $400, with Kito at −$686 the deepest underwater — partly because the league’s 27.0 tally (DHMOTW-inflated) set the HMOTW fee at $270 per manager, the highest ever, and Kito earned back none of it.

2025.title: 2025: The Aidan Era Begins
2025.subtitle: One year after making his debut, Aidan didn’t just improve — he seized first place in Week 5 and never let go, holding the top spot for fourteen straight weeks to win the standings, leading the league in HMOTW tally and sweeping the sidebet pool in a sophomore performance that announced a new force in the league.
body: 🏜️ In his first season Aidan had finished 9th. In his second he finished first — and made it look inevitable. After a quiet four-week opening where Tony and Hanh briefly held the top spot, Aidan posted a 213.22 in Week 5 for his first DHMOTW and grabbed first place. He never gave it back. From Week 5 through Week 18 Aidan held the lead for 14 straight weeks, finishing at 2,909.04 points and becoming the second-youngest champion in league tenure.

🔥 The weekly battles belonged to Aidan too. He led the league in HMOTW tally at 7.0, including three doubled pots: Wk 5 (213.22), Wk 7 (215.84), and Wk 12 (205.72). His season high of 215.84 is the 5th-highest single-week score through 2025. The season produced five DHMOTW weeks total; the most dramatic was Week 15, where Kito (210.32) edged Hanh (209.00) by just 1.32 points for the doubled pot — both cleared 200, only Kito collected.

🏁 Behind Aidan, the race for the podium was tight. Kevin held 2nd for most of the back half, finishing at 2,749.38. Damian made a late push to claim 3rd at 2,740.72, just 8.66 points behind Kevin. Tony rounded out the money in 4th (2,706.10), collecting a 4.0 HMOTW tally along the way. The defending champion Randy slipped to 7th (2,622.48) — not a cellar collapse but a meaningful step back from his record-setting 2024.

💥 The season’s most electric moment came from an unlikely source. Tim spent 16 of 18 weeks in last place in the cumulative standings and posted the league’s lowest season average at 132.9 pts/wk. Then in Week 16 he dropped a 231.40 — the 4th-highest single-week score in league history, behind only Kevin’s 256 (2013), Kito’s 235 (2021), and Damian’s 233 (2024). A season-long drought manager posting an all-time top-5 game in a season he otherwise spent at the bottom — pure TNCFL.

💵 Aidan swept the money as completely as he swept the standings. He took the $903.20 season prize, the $250 ring voucher, $700 in HMOTW earnings, and the $1,000 sidebet pool as the highest cumulative scorer — a net of +$2,183.20. In the playoff bracket, 9 of 10 managers paid in for a $450 pool. The bracket produced the season’s best subplot: Damian, who finished 3rd in the standings, won the playoff crown for $350 — his best payday since his 2012 championship year.

🦧 Two stories lived in the drought column. Kito broke a 33-week desert with a monster Week 15 DHMOTW (210.32), rallying from 2024’s statistical catastrophe to finish 5th — a genuine comeback. And deep in the inactive wilderness, Mikey’s streak quietly climbed to 95 weeks — one short of Bao’s all-time record of 96. The record approaches. Meanwhile Ted closed the season with a 24-week active drought and the league’s second-worst net at −$656, the longest dry run among active managers and a 0.0 tally to go with it.

2011.body:
🌵 Ladies and gentlemen, your inaugural drought king: La. He won a High Man crown early, got a taste of glory in Week 4, and then the heavens sealed shut for fourteen straight weeks 🏜️. Fourteen. He closed the founding season the way a cactus closes a real estate deal — bone dry and going nowhere. Somewhere around Week 9 the rain dance stopped being a joke and became a medical necessity, and still: nothing. Not a drop. The fantasy gods looked down at La's footwork and sent a weather advisory for continued aridity.

🩰 On his tail and praying for their own monsoon: Lonny (11 weeks dry since Week 7 — the man who won three in a row early and has been doing interpretive drought-dance ever since) and Bao (8 weeks and counting, presumably because he was still on the clock from the draft). But make no mistake — this is La's desert. He owns the lease. Lace up the dancing shoes, La. Stomp like the sprinklers depend on it. They do.

2012.body:
🏜️ Welcome to The Mo-BAO-vi Desert — the most desolate expanse in the known fantasy world, named for its sole permanent resident: Bao. He came on La's tail at the end of 2011 sitting on an 8-week dry spell, and rather than do anything about it, he simply… kept going. And going. Through the offseason, through the draft (where he was, naturally, still on the clock 🚬), and clean across all of 2012, until the counter read twenty-five straight weeks without a High Man crown 💀. Twenty-five. That is not a drought, that is a geological era. Rivers have formed and dried up in less time than Bao has gone without a weekly win.

🌧️ The man needs more than dancing shoes — he needs a full ceremonial rain summoning, a sacrificial offering, and possibly a priest. He has been doing the rain dance so long the steps have calcified into the local folklore, and still the fantasy gods withhold the clouds out of what can only be described as personal spite.

👟 Sniffing around the dunes with their own canteens running low: Tony (13 weeks dry since Week 5) and Kito (11 weeks since Week 7, already auditioning for a heartbreak streak that will define his entire career). But this season belongs to Bao and Bao alone. Pour one out — he certainly can't make it rain himself.

2013.body:
🏜️ Remember last year, when we said Kito was auditioning for a heartbreak streak that would define his career? He got the part. Welcome to The A-KITO-cama Desert — modeled after the driest place on planet Earth, and frankly an insult to the Atacama, which at least gets fog. Kito's drought started back in 2012 Week 7, survived the entire offseason, and rolled straight through 2013 to a staggering twenty-eight weeks 💀 — the longest active dry spell the league has ever produced. He didn't just inherit Bao's crown; he beat the record, three weeks deeper into the sand.

🌵 Here's the cruelest part: in Week 14 of 2011, Kito dropped a 168-point bomb, the highest single score of that whole season. The man is capable of biblical weeks. He simply chooses to schedule them at random, years apart, between geologic epochs of nothing. The dancing shoes are worn through to the sock. The fantasy gods have stopped even pretending to watch.

👟 Two rookies are already learning the steps behind him — Damian and Daniel, deadlocked at 17 weeks apiece, both bone-dry since the season opener. But this is Kito's wasteland, the deepest hole anyone has dug. Keep dancing, Kito. At this point the league would settle for a single cloud out of pity.

2014.body:
🏜️ The A-KITO-cama Desert is now entering its third calendar year, and Kito remains its only citizen, its mayor, and its sole climate refugee. That same drought that started in 2012 Week 7 — the one we crowned as a record at 28 weeks last season — did not break. It did not slow. It is now forty-five weeks deep 💀, a dry spell so long it predates relationships, outlives houseplants, and is rapidly approaching the gestation period of an elephant. Kito has gone the better part of three full seasons without a single High Man crown.

🌧️ At this point the rain dance has evolved into something closer to a religion — and Kito is its lone, increasingly desperate priest, stomping in the dust while the fantasy gods file a restraining order. He still posts the occasional monster week. It still never lands on the right one. The cruelty is so precise it has to be intentional.

👟 New faces are migrating into the wasteland behind him: Douang (21 weeks dry since 2013 Week 14) and Kevin (17 weeks, winless the entire season). They're learning what Kito learned years ago — that out here, the sprinklers are a myth. But make no mistake: this is still Kito's kingdom of dust, and the lease shows no sign of expiring.

2015.body:
🏜️ With Kito's reign finally rained out, the drought crown passes to its patient understudy. Welcome to The Douango Desert, and its sun-baked landlord, Douang. Here's the cruel comedy of it: Douang had a genuinely good 2015 — a top-five finish — yet hasn't tasted a single High Man crown since 2013 Week 14. That's thirty-eight weeks dry 💀, a drought he quietly nursed in Kito's shadow for two full years until the music stopped and he was the last man standing without a chair.

🌧️ He is living proof of the league's oldest law: you can score all season and still never win a week. Douang puts up points, finishes respectably, and the weekly crown sails past him every single time like he's standing behind glass. The dancing shoes are out of the box, Douang. The gods are watching. They are, as ever, unmoved.

👟 Trudging through the same dunes: Randy (21 weeks dry since his 2014 title run cooled off) and La (18 weeks, fresh off a last-place campaign). But the deed to this desert is Douang's. Stomp, Douang. Stomp like the box score depends on it.

2016.body:
🏜️ A new tenant takes the lease. Welcome to The So-TONY-ran Desert — and its parched proprietor, Tony. The whiplash here is something special: just one season ago Tony finished second overall and led the league with four weekly crowns. He was the breakout star. Then the taps shut off. He hasn't won a High Man since 2015 Week 12 — twenty-three weeks dry 💀 — and slid all the way to 9th for his trouble. From the silver podium to the sand in the span of a calendar.

🌧️ This is the Curse's favorite trick: hand a man a great year, let him taste it, then quietly turn the season into a desert behind him. Tony's been dancing since the back half of 2015 and the sky has answered with nothing but a dry, indifferent breeze. Lace 'em up tighter, Tony.

👟 Sharing the heat: Kito (19 weeks dry — yes, already relapsing barely a year after his record drought finally broke) and Hanh (16 weeks, winless since Week 2). But the So-TONY-ran is Tony's to roam. Somewhere out there is a cloud with his name on it. It is in no hurry.

2017.body:
🏜️ The deed changes hands again, and this time the new landlord has a champion's pedigree. Behold The Sa-RANDY Desert — vast, ancient, and presided over by Randy, the same man who walked in as a rookie and won the whole league in 2014. How the mighty dry out. Randy hasn't claimed a single High Man crown since 2016 Week 9 — that's twenty-six weeks of nothing 💀 — the longest active drought in the league, and a long, sandy fall from the kid who once made it rain points on everybody.

🌧️ There's a cruel poetry to it: the rookie who arrived like a monsoon now can't summon a drop. He stomps, he dances, he checks the forecast — and the fantasy gods, who once handed him a title gift-wrapped, now won't return his calls. Three years is a long time to wait for weather.

👟 Kicking up dust behind him: Tony (13 weeks dry, a permanent resident of these parts by now) and Damian (12 weeks, the reigning former champ cooling off). But the Sa-RANDY belongs to Randy. Dance, champ. The sky remembers your title even if it refuses to reward it.

2018.body:
🏜️ He told you he was a permanent resident. The So-TONY-ran Desert reopens under its original and only proprietor, Tony, who has now turned a long-term lease into outright ownership. While Randy escaped the sand and rode it all the way to a title, Tony stayed behind and kept right on baking: his drought now stretches a brutal thirty weeks 💀, dating back to 2017 Week 5. He capped it by finishing dead last in the league's highest-scoring season ever — a special kind of cruelty, to go winless in a year when everyone else was hanging 200s.

🌧️ Picture it: six different managers detonated for 200-plus in 2018, the points were falling like monsoon rain all around him, and not a single drop landed on Tony's roof. The man is standing in a thunderstorm holding an empty bucket. The dancing has become less a ritual than a cry for help.

👟 Also parched, though nowhere near the landlord: Douang (25 weeks, a familiar face in these dunes) and Hanh (18 weeks, the 2017 champ cooling off fast). But this is the So-TONY-ran, and Tony isn't going anywhere. Stomp, Tony. Stomp like it's the only thing left.

2019.body:
🏜️ The forecast for Kevinsburg reads the same every single week: severe drought watch, zero percent chance of a crown, highs near unbearable. Welcome to The Ke-VIN-pty Quarter, the league's newest and emptiest stretch of sand, presided over by Kevin — a former champion now surveying a kingdom of dust. He hasn't hoisted a High Man crown since 2018 Week 14, and the meter has run all the way to twenty-one bone-dry weeks 💀, over a full season without a drop. He capped it with a 9th-place finish, because the desert likes to take the standings down with it.

🌧️ And what a cruel year to stay parched. 2019 was the season the rain finally came for everyone ELSE: Bao walked in and washed away a 96-week record drought, Tony broke a 38-week dry spell, the skies opened over Tonyville and Baosburg and LaLa Land alike. The whole league got soaked. Kevin stood in the middle of the monsoon, arms outstretched, voodoo doll in one hand and an empty bucket in the other — and not one drop found him. At this point the rain dance isn't a ritual; it's a cry for help.

👟 Kicking up dust at the edge of the Quarter: a familiar face in Bao (13 weeks dry already, the ink barely set on his comeback) and even Randy (10 weeks, the league's erstwhile rainmaker gone suddenly quiet). But the deed says Kevin, and the Ke-VIN-pty Quarter is open for business. Lace up, Kevin. Stomp, twirl, beg, bring out the voodoo dolls — the whole routine. The sky owes you nothing and intends to pay every penny of it.

2020.body:
🏜️ Gather round for the cruelest weather report in league history. The Sa-RANDY Desert has reopened under its original landlord, Randy — and oh, how far the man has fallen. Rewind a single year: in 2019 Randy led the league in first place for fifteen straight weeks, won five early crowns, swept the side pot, and stood as the all-time money leader of the entire league. He was the rainmaker. He was the forecast. Now he's the dust bowl. Randy hasn't felt a drop since 2019 Week 8 — twenty-seven bone-dry weeks 💀, the longest active drought in the league — and capped 2020 dead last in earnings. From rainmaker to rain-beggar in twelve short months.

🌧️ And he danced for it, believe me. Through a whole pandemic season the man tried every step in the book — the rain dance, the twerkquake, the naked dance, the forbidden Lambada — and the sky just laughed and turned up the thermostat. In Week 17 he finally summoned a 206-point monster, surely enough to break the spell — except La went and scored 211 the same week and stole the crown right out from under him. Randy didn't end his drought; he just joined the most exclusive club of misery in the league: 200 points and STILL no High Man. The desert wasn't even his worst luck that day.

👟 Baking right alongside him: Ted (26 weeks dry, his own MonTE Desert a mere week behind Randy's), the sophomore who hasn't seen rain since his rookie campaign. The two of them have turned the bottom of the drought chart into a duplex. But the deed says Randy, and the Sa-RANDY is the largest, driest, most ironic patch of sand in the league. Lace up, champ. You once made it pour on everybody. Now do it for yourself — the forecast says you've forgotten how.

2021.body:
🏜️ Every league needs a cautionary tale, and 2021 handed us a rookie who wrote his on arrival. Welcome to Tim Buck Two — a remote, sun-blasted outpost on the very edge of the map, founded and ruled by Tim, who managed the rare feat of going his entire 18-week debut season without a single drop of rain 💀. Not one High Man crown. Eighteen weeks, zero precipitation, a drought that started in Week 1 and simply never ended. While his fellow rookie Titi was busy leading the league for sixteen straight weeks and lapping the field, Tim was out back in Tim Buck Two, watering a cactus and calling it farming.

🌧️ There's a cruel comedy to a man arriving in the desert the same year another arrival builds a palace. Same draft, same rules, same waiver wire — one rookie left with a ring and the fattest debut payday in league history, the other left with sand in his shoes and a 9th-place finish. Tim, the forecast for your rookie year was a goose egg under a heat lamp. Pack the rain dance, the twerkquake, the whole routine — you're going to need all of it in year two.

👟 Sharing the dunes, of all people: Kito (17 weeks dry), the deposed king himself. One year removed from a 222-point eruption and a silver medal, the 2019 champion plummeted to dead last and now bakes beside a winless rookie — the odd couple of the desert, the man who had everything and the man who never got started. But the newest deed says Tim, and Tim Buck Two is open for business. Lace up, rookie. The sky has been ignoring you since the day you walked in.

2022.body:
🏜️ Ladies and gentlemen, the rain dance returns to a familiar address. Last year we introduced you to Tim Buck Two, the sun-blasted outpost on the edge of the map where Tim spent his entire 18-week rookie season without a single drop of rain. We assumed it was a one-year lease. We were wrong. Tim renewed, expanded, and broke ground on a second wing 💧. Eighteen more weeks, eighteen more cloudless skies, and the drought that began in his very first career game now stretches an unbroken 36 weeks — officially the longest earned-while-active drought in the entire league. Not a sprinkle. Not a mist. Not one High Man crown across two full seasons. The man could host a sandcastle convention.

He's got company on the dunes, mind you. Ted finished a respectable 3rd in the standings and still went home with 26 dry weeks in his luggage — proof you can make the money and still forget your umbrella. D'lyn is parched too, at 22 weeks and counting. But neither holds the deed. Tim Buck Two is Tim's town, and business is booming in the worst possible way.

So lace them up, Tim. The dancing shoes are back out of the box, the sky is a merciless, cloudless blue, and the fantasy gods have apparently put you on permanent mute. Somewhere out there is a rain cloud with your name on it. Keep dancing — year three is going to need it.

2023.body:
🏜️ Welcome back to the rain-dance stage. We’ve had first-timers, we’ve had repeat offenders — but we’ve never had a reigning champion lace up the dancing shoes. Until now. Ladies and gentlemen, please welcome Tony: the man who waited eleven seasons for his first ring, got it in 2022, celebrated all winter, and then came back and wandered straight back into the So-TONY-ran Desert without a single High Man crown in 18 consecutive weeks.

Let’s review the numbers. Tony went 0 HMOTW tallies in 2023. Zero. Goose egg. He had 21 straight dry weeks entering the offseason, the longest active drought in the league by a comfortable margin. He finished 6th in the standings, which is a respectable middle-of-the-pack showing but is also, let’s be honest, not what a defending champion is supposed to look like. The 2022 version of Tony led 16 of 18 weeks. The 2023 version couldn’t lead a single one of them for long enough to count.

The cruelest part? The season belonged entirely to a man who had been Tony’s rain-dance understudy for two full years. Tim came in with a 36-week drought, won everything in sight, and left with the ring Tony was defending. While Tim was pocketing $2,232, Tony was posting -$564 and watching from the middle of the table.

So here we are. The crown is gone, the weekly pots never arrived, and the So-TONY-ran Desert has reclaimed its namesake. The deed never left his name — the championship just made him forget it for a year. The dancing shoes fit, the sky is a familiar cloudless blue, and the fantasy gods have a very particular sense of humor. Lace up, champ. You’ve earned this one.

2024.body:
🏜️ Some seasons the rain-dance picks itself. Kito in 2024 didn’t just have a drought — he had a full statistical catastrophe. Let’s count the ways. Zero HMOTW tallies in 18 weeks. Not one crown, not one tie, not one week where he was the last man standing. The doubled-pot era has been active since 2016 and Kito has a career tally of 40.5 — but in 2024 he collected exactly none of it.

10th place in the final standings at 2,394.50. He spent 11 of 18 weeks in last place in the cumulative standings — meaning for more than half the season, every single other manager in this league had more points than he did. His season avg was 133.0 pts/wk, lowest in the league by an 8-point margin. His drought entering the offseason: 33 weeks and climbing.

The cruelest detail? This is the same Kito who ended a 53-week drought in 2015 with a Week 9 crown and spent years as one of the league’s most dangerous weekly scorers. The Monday-Night Miracle from Hawaii is on the books. The 235.48 in 2021 is the 2nd-highest score all-time. The ceiling is real. The 2024 floor, unfortunately, was also very real.

So lace them up, Kito. The 33-week desert is yours, the HMOTW ledger has a big goose egg next to your name, and the fantasy gods spent 18 Thursdays pretending you didn’t exist. The dancing shoes have been waiting. They still fit.

2025.body:
🏜️ Pull up a chair, because Ted has been standing in this particular desert for a while now. Twenty-four weeks. No crown. No tally. Not a single High Man moment across an entire season and change. The dancing shoes have been waiting by the door since Week 3 of 2024, and Ted just… never picked them up.

Let’s talk numbers, because the numbers deserve to be talked about. 0.0 HMOTW tally in 2025. Ted was the only manager in the league who didn’t collect a single crown or half-crown all season. He finished 9th at 2,570.38 with a season avg of 142.8 pts/wk — which is not embarrassing on its own, but when everyone around you is winning weeks and you’re not, the standings take care of themselves.

The cruelest detail: Ted was the busiest waiver-wire man not named Aidan, making 38 transactions hunting for an edge that never came. All that movement, all those pickups, all those Thursdays — and the HMOTW pot never once landed in his lap. His net for the season: −$656, the worst in the league.

So here we are. The 24-week drought is the longest active streak in the league, the ledger is deep red, and somewhere out there is a rain cloud with Ted’s name on it. It’s been 24 Thursdays. Lace up.

2011.title: 🎲 Five Kings, One Crown
2011.body: The founding season was pure anarchy at the top: five different managers held first place at some point — Kito, La, Lonny, Bao, and finally Hanh — across 8 lead changes in just 17 weeks. La and Kito each spent 5 weeks on the throne, Bao 4, Lonny 1, and Hanh just 2. Nobody owned 2011 until the very last man to grab the lead refused to give it back.

2011.title: 🥷 The Two-Week Champion
2011.body: Here's how little the standings meant before the finish: Hanh won the title while leading just 2 of 17 weeks. He sat in dead last (6th) for five different weeks — and was still in last place as late as Week 12 — before vaulting to first in Week 16 and never looking back. The first champion of the Curse spent more of the season in the cellar than on the throne.

2011.title: 🚬 Bao's Four-Week Throne
2011.body: The slowest drafter in league history briefly ran the whole thing: Bao seized first place in Week 9 and held it four straight weeks (Weeks 9–12) — the longest single reign of the founding season. Then came the deflation. His Week 12 score of 90 was a 15% drop from his Week 11, the throne wobbled, and Kito pounced. Bao's deliberation bought him a reign; it couldn't buy him the title.

2011.title: 🔪 A 30-Point Logjam
2011.body: The 3rd-through-5th spots were a knife fight: Mikey (1,817), Bao (1,800), and La (1,787) finished within just 30 points of each other.

2011.title: 🎯 Kito's 168 — The First Record
2011.body: Kito detonated for 168 points in Week 14 — the season's High Man crown, the single biggest game of 2011, and the all-time league single-week record as the founding year closed. He carried that firepower to a 1,924-point finish… and still lost the title by 28. The most points, the least to show for it — Kito's heartbreak résumé starts here.

2011.title: 💰 The Founding Economics
2011.body: On the original $100 buy-in, champion Hanh banked +$481 while last-place Lonny ate -$109 — the founding season's first lesson that the curse costs money, not just pride.

2012.title: ⚔️ A Two-Man War — and a Rookie Sweep
2012.body: Year two doubled the league to ten, and the newcomers seized it instantly: only Damian and Douang ever held first place all season, just 3 lead changes in 17 weeks. Douang clung to the top as late as Week 10 before Damian took over for good, leading 12 of 17 weeks.
